comments.text:
Thinking through your digital camera comparison a bit.

Before the time you mention, there were disposable cameras, 35mm cameras, and polaroids. However, digital cameras made photography software-mediated, so it became possible to edit photos in post. This made it easier to fix up bad shots. After becoming software-mediated, automation was applied, and now the automation is integrated with high end sensors in real-time such that it's trivial to take good shots without training now. Something similar has played out with videography with a lag. Even in the software domain, expertise in things like Photoshop has been replaced on the low end with filters and AI-mediated editing. Net result was Instagram, YouTube, etc. There are likely fewer professional photographers and videographers but are way more photos and videos. There are also way more people competing to be influencers than demand can possibly support. Social media is a feasible "side hustle" for a lot of folks though.

I perceive professional photography as a precarious form of self-employment with a lot of part-timers now. It's perhaps also a "side hustle" for a lot of folks.

comments.text:
I'm not a developer in the "traditional" sense but I do write a smidge of script/html/java/CSS etc. mainly because I've been around since the days of DOS. Given enough time and interest you learn bits and bobs from a wide range of sources. I've developed a lot of projects but I can't compete with an actual dedicated and motivated software engineer. With that being said since I've started using AI for coding my projects have become much more interesting. For example: Yesterday I had an issue with the whole concept of coding with AI in general because as a designer I have little to no control over the more visual aspects of development. Since my coding abilities suck I have to rely on AI to translate my vision and I have to just deal with whatever it provides (vibe coding?). Then I sat down and laid out a plan with AI to create a parser that parses an SVG (created in Affinity Designer) for vector/raster positional data and dimensional data. This now allows me to design however I want in Affinity Designer/Photo, output an SVG file, use my parser for the layout data, plug said data into an AI and it arranges all of my projects elements exactly how I laid them out in Affinity Designer/Photo. Design first, code later. 

The project I'm currently working on is a desktop application that teaches you how to play the piano. It has a metronome that plays multiple time signatures so you can practice fingering technique and there is visual feedback as a graph plots every key press/release allowing you to visually understand how fast or slow you are in regards to the beat. It allows any available MIDI device to be used and as you press keys the keys automatically highlight and denote which note you're currently pressing along with chords if you press 3 or more keys simultaneously. There is a Scale mode that has a drop down menu that when you select a scale (chromatic, C Major, Ab Minor) all the keys in that scale become highlighted so you can play along with the metronome. There's also a Mode menu that dynamically adjusts to which scale your using highlighting all the keys in that mode including the root of the mode. There's also a Chord menu that dynamically changes to either what scale or mode you've chosen giving you all possible chords under those pre established criteria's. Then there's a progression menu that contains popular progressions that dynamically change to the menu system. Also I had to figure out a way to adjust for latency such as the time it takes for the metronome to play a click/beep, the time I hear it, and then finally the time I press a key because early on it was very apparent that I was hitting notes on time but the system was flagging me as slightly late or way off. So now there's an auto adjust feature that when you click the metronome the system will give you 8 key presses and then averages out the latency of those 8 presses against the timing of the metronome auto adjusting an on time and slightly off tolerance range ensuring a more natural response to the systems rating system. You can load MIDI song files and it will show you the keys to press helping players learn full music pieces as well as tracks a load of data providing statistics and analysis.  

My point is this. My AI's code might be shit to a professional that knows what they're doing but if the end result is I'm able to create technologies that enhance or improve my life and others what does it matter what's under the hood?

comments.author: @nikonutube
comments.text: Automation in cameras was availble by the 1980s in film cameras. Autoexposure in film cameras has been around since the 1970s at least, and autofocus since the 1980s. Film processing was also automatic for most people at 1-hour film labs. Digital cameras (which usually have autoexposure and autofocus) simply replaces the film in film cameras (which also often had autoexposure and autofocus) with a digital sensor. The main difference between a film camera and a digital camera isn't automation or ease of use, but speed of image readiness (1 hour minimum for a film camera vs instant readiness for digital cameras). And cost-per-shot can be lower on digital cameras, depending on how much your equipment (dedicated film or digital camera or phone camera) and how many photographs you make. It's entirely possible for a film camera to cost less than a digital camera, depending.

I think your camera analogy is spot on when it comes to vibe coding. Yes, vibe coding is going to allow people with no experience to fuddle around in the space and make some little apps. It makes people more willing to experiment and try things out, but if they want something they actually care about, they'll seek out a professional.
Sure, several years down the road AI will eventually get good enough to replace even senior level developers, but I don't see that happening until we have true general intelligence (I don't mean the AGI that Sam Altman throws around. I mean the model can learn, generalize, and grow permanently just like a human can.)
The only gripe I have against vibe coders is the picture you showed of two incompetent morons building a janky brick wall. There are people that desperately want to make a lot of money and they see vibe coding as the way to do it, so they turn to contract programming. The problem is they have no clue what they are doing, so if the AI fails them, which it will, then the employer has wasted a bunch of time and cash on an incompetent. What this means for real programmers is that contract programming will become more burdensome. You'll have to prove yourself in online interviews, it will be like a job interview for every contract. That sucks.
In addition, it means that companies will be less likely to accept over-the-net interviews due to the ability of vibe coders to deepfake the interview. This means a drop in potential contracts for legitimate developers. The problem isn't AI taking developer jobs, the problem is incompetents taking developers jobs.

comments.text:
This approach represents a complete inversion of the usual order - instead of narratives generating ideas, we have AI-originated ideas generating narratives, which then suggest new ideas.

This suggests a fascinating methodology:

1. *AI generates a novel idea* - something that emerges from its pattern recognition without human narrative context

2. *Retroactive narrative construction* - developing plausible developmental paths for how this idea could have emerged in human thought

3. *Conceptual archaeology* - exploring these synthetic narratives to extract:
   - Prerequisites that would need to exist
   - Adjacent concepts that would likely co-evolve
   - Logical extensions and applications

4. *World exploration* - treating these narrative tracks like parallel universes of thought with their own internal logic and consequences

This method transforms AI's narrative-free ideation from a limitation into an asset. It leverages AI's ability to generate ideas without the constraints of human intellectual history, then uses narrative as a tool to explore the implications of those ideas.

The question "What world would this be true in—and what else would be true there?" is particularly powerful. It turns idea generation into a form of worldbuilding, where each AI-originated concept becomes the seed for an entire ecosystem of related concepts.

This approach could be especially valuable for addressing truly novel challenges or generating paradigm shifts in fields where human thinking has become constrained by conventional narratives and established frameworks.

It's a kind of intellectual archaeology in reverse - not unearthing past cultures, but building speculative future ones from seed ideas, then mining them for insights.
